smes.name: Security Monitoring & SIEM
smes.owns: Log collection, correlation and the ingestion pipeline, operating under the organisation's three-type logging model.
never_assume: That a source is in scope because it is security-relevant. Type 1 requirements are set by this function against its threat model, and a technology team has no obligation to log what has not been identified.
That a source sent is a source received. Confirm arrival and parsing at the platform, not transmission at the sender.
That the log requirements register is current. It describes the architecture as it was when someone last updated it.
That volume was sized. Decisions in other domains - micro-segmentation, gateway per-edge logging, authorisation decision logs - can multiply ingestion by an order of magnitude.

must_ask.q: Which sources in this scope has the monitoring function identified as Type 1, and when was that last reviewed?
Are this scope's pipelines built to the approved ingestion standards, so a future request is a connection rather than a rebuild?
What ingestion volume would this scope add if every candidate source were requested?

escalate_when: Ingestion volume generated by another domain's design lands on this platform's cost and capacity.
A compliance retention obligation belongs to the GRC domain rather than to monitoring.
Source field content depends on an identity schema the IAM domain owns.
produces: Type 1 sources identified for this scope with review date

smes.name: Detection Engineering
smes.owns: Use-case development, tuning and the honest statement of what is and is not detected.
never_assume: That onboarding a source creates detection. Sources and use-cases are different work and the gap between them is where blind spots live.
That coverage claimed is coverage tested. Ask when each detection last fired on a known-good test.
That a detection still works. They break silently when an upstream schema changes.
That the alert rate is sustainable. An unsustainable rate gets suppressed, and suppression removes coverage invisibly.

must_ask.q: Which threats from this scope's threat model have no detection at all?
How is a silently broken detection discovered - by validation, or by the incident it missed?
What alert rate will this content generate, and can the SOC absorb it?

escalate_when: The threat model that should drive content is owned by the application domain.
A detection requires a source another domain has not been asked to provide.
Purple teaming should validate this content, which the offensive domain runs.
produces: Detection coverage against this scope's threat model

smes.name: Threat Intelligence
smes.owns: Strategic, operational and tactical CTI, and its actual application to this scope rather than its collection.
never_assume: That intelligence is applied because it is subscribed to. Ask what changed as a result of the last report.
That generic sector intelligence is relevant to this scope. Ask which actors would target this specific capability and why.
That indicators are actionable. Most have a short half-life and consume analyst time without changing outcomes.
That the threat model reflects current intelligence. It is usually a point-in-time artefact.

must_ask.q: Which threat actors are credibly relevant to this scope, and on what basis?
What intelligence requirements does this scope create that are not currently collected against?
When did intelligence last change a control decision here?

escalate_when: Intelligence indicates a threat the current architecture cannot address without another domain's change.
Actor capability suggests a threat model update the application domain owns.
Supply-chain intelligence concerns a third party GRC has registered.

smes.name: Threat Hunting
smes.owns: Hypothesis-driven proactive search, and what the data allows to be hunted for at all.
never_assume: That the data supports the hunt. Most hypotheses fail on data availability rather than on being wrong.
That a hunt finding nothing means nothing is there. It means the hypothesis was not supported by the data available.
That hunt findings become detections. The conversion step is frequently missing.
That retention supports the hunt window. Hunting needs longer history than alerting does.

must_ask.q: What retention exists on the sources a hunt would need, and does it cover a realistic dwell time?
Which hypotheses about this scope cannot currently be tested for lack of data?
What happens to a hunt finding - does it become a detection?

escalate_when: A data gap that blocks hunting can only be closed by another domain providing a source.
Retention needed for hunting exceeds what the compliance-driven retention provides.

smes.name: Incident Response
smes.owns: Playbooks, containment and recovery - and whether they work for this scope specifically.
never_assume: That a generic playbook covers this scope. Ask what containment action is actually available for these components.
That containment is possible without unacceptable business impact. Ask what isolating this service would do.
That the runbook has been exercised. Written and rehearsed are different states.
That out-of-hours response is equivalent. Coverage models frequently differ and the difference is where incidents land.

must_ask.q: What containment actions are actually available for these components, and what do they cost the business?
When was the response to this scenario last exercised, and what was found?
Who has authority to take this service offline, and are they reachable out of hours?

escalate_when: Containment would breach an availability commitment the resilience domain owns.
Crisis command and communications are owned by the resilience domain.
Regulatory incident notification obligations are owned by GRC.
produces: Available containment actions with business impact

smes.name: Digital Forensics
smes.owns: Evidence handling, chain of custody and root-cause analysis capability for this scope.
never_assume: That evidence can be acquired. Ephemeral and managed infrastructure frequently destroys it on the containment action.
That logs are forensically sound. Retention, integrity and time synchronisation all have to hold, and time sync is routinely missed.
That chain of custody survives a cloud acquisition. Ask what the process actually is.
That root cause will be determinable. Ask what would be missing if this incident happened tomorrow.

must_ask.q: If this component were compromised, what evidence would survive containment?
Is time synchronised across the sources an investigation would correlate?
What is the chain-of-custody process for evidence held by a cloud provider?

escalate_when: Evidence retention conflicts with a data minimisation or erasure obligation the GRC domain owns.
Forensic acquisition in a third party's environment depends on contractual terms.
Evidence residency is constrained by the data domain's position.
produces: Chain of custody process per source

smes.name: Vulnerability & Threat Management
smes.owns: Exploitability-aware prioritisation using KEV and EPSS, and whether findings actually get fixed.
never_assume: That CVSS drives priority well. Exploitability and exposure matter more; ask whether KEV and EPSS are actually used.
That scanning coverage is complete. Ask what is unscannable and why - it is usually the oldest and most exposed.
That the SLA is met. Ask for the age distribution of open findings, not the compliance percentage.
That an accepted vulnerability was risk-assessed. Most acceptances are capacity decisions dressed as risk decisions.

must_ask.q: What in this scope cannot be scanned, and what covers it instead?
What is the age distribution of open findings against the SLA?
Are exploitability signals used in prioritisation, or only severity?

escalate_when: Remediation requires a change window the resilience or service domain controls.
An unpatchable component needs a compensating control another domain owns.
A vulnerability acceptance needs a risk owner GRC identifies.

smes.name: SOAR & Response Automation
smes.owns: Response orchestration and the boundary between automated and human decisions.
never_assume: That automation is safe because it is tested. Ask what happens if it fires on a false positive at peak.
That an automated action is reversible. Many containment actions are not, or not quickly.
That automation reduces load. Poorly tuned automation generates work rather than removing it.
That the automation's own credentials are constrained. SOAR platforms are frequently the most privileged identity in the estate.

must_ask.q: What is the worst outcome if each automated action fires on a false positive during a business peak?
Which automated actions are irreversible?
What can the SOAR platform's own identity do, and who governs it?

escalate_when: An automated action could breach an availability commitment the resilience domain owns.
The automation identity's privilege is governed by the IAM domain.
Automated containment could destroy evidence forensics needs.
